name: Korean Grammar Drill
credits: Hand-curated to complement the TOPIK 1 vocab path. Sequenced from orthography (hangul block structure) through morphology (particles, conjugation, honorifics). Common-error notes drawn from published L2-Korean error corpora (NIKL Anglophone learner corpus, Sogang/Yonsei error notes) and from typical Talk To Me In Korean / How To Study Korean classroom feedback.

units.title: Hangul block structure — how syllables are built
units.goal: Decompose any hangul syllable into its consonant and vowel components, and assemble new ones from parts.
units.explanation: Hangul is alphabetic but visually syllabic: every block is exactly one syllable. A block has 2 or 3 slots — an initial consonant (초성), a vowel (중성), and an optional final consonant (종성, called 받침 'support'). Vertical vowels like ㅏ ㅓ ㅣ go to the RIGHT of the initial consonant; horizontal vowels like ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ go BELOW it. A final consonant sits at the bottom. Silent ㅇ fills the initial slot when a syllable starts with a vowel sound (아, 이, 우) — it has no sound there, only the role of a placeholder. Korean has 14 basic consonants, 10 basic vowels, and a set of double consonants (ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ) and diphthongs.

endings.ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ: 한 (han) — initial ㅎ, vowel ㅏ to the right, final ㄴ below
endings.ㄱ + ㅗ: 고 (go) — initial ㄱ, vowel ㅗ below, no final
endings.ㅇ + ㅣ: 이 (i) — silent ㅇ placeholder, vowel ㅣ to the right

examples.en: silent + a = the vowel 'a' on its own

examples.target: ㅅ + ㅏ + ㄴ + ㄱ = 산 + 강 = 산강

common_errors: Writing hangul left-to-right as a flat alphabet (ㅎㅏㄴ instead of 한) — letters MUST be stacked into the block shape
Forgetting the silent ㅇ in vowel-initial syllables — 'I' is 이, never just ㅣ
Putting a vertical vowel (ㅏ ㅓ) below the consonant or a horizontal vowel (ㅗ ㅜ) to the right — orientation is fixed
Treating double consonants (ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ) as 'twice as loud' — they're tensed, not doubled in sound

drill.prompt: Combine ㅁ + ㅗ + ㄹ into a block.
Combine ㅇ + ㅓ + ㅁ + ㅁ + ㅏ into two blocks (mother, casual).
Decompose 사람 (person) into blocks then letters.
Which is correctly written: ㅎㅏㄴ or 한?
drill.answer: 한 — letters must stack into the block.

drill.prompt: Build the block for the sound 'go'.
drill.answer: 고 (ㄱ over ㅗ — horizontal vowel goes below)

drill.prompt: Build the block for the sound 'ga' (vowel ㅏ).
drill.answer: 가 (ㄱ to the left of ㅏ — vertical vowel goes to the right)

units.title: Sentence-final endings — speech levels (해 / 해요 / 합니다)
units.goal: Choose between intimate (해체), polite (해요체), and formal (합쇼체) speech levels appropriately.
units.explanation: Every Korean sentence ends in a verb (or stative adjective), and every verb commits to one of seven speech levels. Beginners only need three: 해 (해체, intimate — same age close friends, family younger than you, lovers), 해요 (해요체, polite informal — the universal default for strangers, coworkers, anyone older or higher status when you don't need to be ceremonious), and 합니다 (합쇼체, formal — news, military, presentations, customer-facing service, first meetings). The level is locked in at the end of the verb stem. Using 해 to a stranger is rude; using 합니다 to a close friend is cold and weird. When in doubt, 해요 is safe.

endings.polite (해요체): 가요 (statement / question / suggestion / mild command — intonation distinguishes)

examples.en: Where are you going? (to a close friend)
Where are you going? (formal, often + honorific)

common_errors: Switching levels mid-conversation — once you commit to 해요 with someone, stay there until you both downshift to 해
Using 해 (intimate) with anyone older or unknown — even a year older is enough in Korean to demand 해요 unless explicitly invited to drop it (반말 해도 돼요?)
Treating 합니다 as the 'most polite, always safe' choice — overusing it sounds robotic / military; 해요 is the everyday register
Asking questions in 합쇼체 with -요 instead of -까 — formal questions take -까, not -요 (갑니까, not 갑니다요)

drill.prompt: You meet your boss for the first time. Choose the right ending for 'I am Mark': 마크____. (이야 / 이에요 / 입니다)
You text your best friend 'where are you?'. Choose: 어디____? (있어 / 있어요 / 있습니까)
You order coffee at a café. Choose: 커피 한 잔 ____. (줘 / 주세요 / 주십시오)
drill.answer: 주세요 (polite is the default service register)

units.title: Topic particles 은/는 vs Subject particles 이/가
units.goal: Choose between the topic marker (은/는) and the subject marker (이/가).
units.explanation: Korean has two ways to flag the noun that anchors a sentence: 은/는 (topic — 'as for X, here's the news') and 이/가 (subject — 'X is the one that...'). 은/는 frames known/contextual information ('about X, here's a comment') and is used for contrast or topic-shift; 이/가 introduces new information or singles out the subject from alternatives (often answering 'who/what?'). Attachment rule: a noun ending in a VOWEL takes 는 / 가; a noun ending in a CONSONANT takes 은 / 이. Beginners can think of 은/는 as Japanese は and 이/가 as Japanese が — the contrast is similar but not identical.

pattern.stem: consonant-end noun + 은 or 이 / vowel-end noun + 는 or 가

examples.target: 저는 학생이에요. (topic — 'as for me, I'm a student')
누가 학생이에요? — 제가 학생이에요. (subject — 'I'M the one who is a student')
examples.en: Who is the student? — I am.
Today, it's raining. (topic = today; subject = rain)
Korea — the food is delicious. (topic + nested subject)
I — I don't like COFFEE (but I might like other things).

common_errors: Defaulting to 은/는 for everything — 'who is hungry?' answer needs 이/가: 저는 배고파요 is fine in isolation, but 'I am (the hungry one)' to that question is 제가 배고파요
Wrong allomorph by attachment — 친구은 (wrong, vowel-end) / 친구는 (correct), 사람가 (wrong, consonant-end) / 사람이 (correct)
Translating both as English 'is' — neither is a copula; the copula is 이다 (이에요/예요)
Forgetting that 저 (I, humble) + 가 has an irregular form: 제가 (not 저가) — same for 너 (you, casual) → 네가

drill.prompt: Answer 'who came?' with 'My friend came.' — 친구___ 왔어요. (이/가)
Translate 'As for today, it's hot.' — 오늘___ 더워요. (은/는)
Fill: 제___ 했어요. ('I'M the one who did it' — irregular)

units.title: Object particles 을/를
units.goal: Mark direct objects correctly using 을 (after consonant) or 를 (after vowel).
units.explanation: Korean direct objects take the particle 을/를 — the answer to 'whom/what does the verb act on?'. Attachment is purely phonological: consonant-end noun → 을, vowel-end noun → 를. Word order is SOV (Subject-Object-Verb), so the object sits between the subject and the verb: 저는 김치를 먹어요 ('I kimchi eat'). In casual speech, 을/를 is frequently dropped; in writing and formal speech it's expected. Don't confuse it with the location particle 에 — 을/를 marks the THING acted on, never the place.

pattern.stem: consonant-end noun + 을 / vowel-end noun + 를

endings.casual drop: 밥 먹어요 (instead of 밥을 먹어요) is fine in speech

examples.en: My friend is reading a book.

examples.target: 영화를 봐요. / 영화 봐요. (dropped in casual)

common_errors: Wrong allomorph — 밥를 (wrong, consonant-end) / 밥을 (correct); 커피을 (wrong, vowel-end) / 커피를 (correct)
Using 을/를 with verbs that aren't transitive in Korean — 만나다 (to meet) takes 을/를 but 도착하다 (to arrive) takes 에 (place), not 를
Putting the object AFTER the verb (English habit) — Korean is rigidly SOV: 'I eat kimchi' = 저는 김치를 먹어요, not 저는 먹어요 김치를
Dropping 을/를 in writing — fine in casual speech, but in essays / formal Korean it's expected

drill.prompt: Order the words: 먹어요 / 김치를 / 저는. Result?
Which particle is dropped in casual speech: 을/를 or 은/는?
drill.answer: Both can drop, but 을/를 drops most frequently.

units.title: Location particles 에 vs 에서
units.explanation: 에 marks the destination of motion (가다, 오다, 도착하다) and the static location of existence (있다, 없다, 살다). 에서 marks the place where an action HAPPENS (먹다, 일하다, 공부하다, 만나다). The English preposition 'at' or 'in' splits in two: 'I'm AT home' = 집에 있어요 (existence, 에); 'I work AT home' = 집에서 일해요 (action, 에서). 에서 can also mean 'from' for departure points: 서울에서 부산까지 (from Seoul to Busan). Both particles attach to any noun without phonological allomorphy — 집에 and 집에서 work the same as 학교에 and 학교에서.

examples.en: I go to the company. (destination → 에)
I work at the company. (action → 에서)
I came from the USA. (departure → 에서)

common_errors: Using 에서 with 있다/없다/살다 — 'I live in Seoul' is 서울에 살아요, not 서울에서 살아요 (살다 is a stative-existence verb here)
Using 에 with action verbs — 'I study at school' is 학교에서 공부해요, NOT 학교에 공부해요
Treating 에 as 'in' and 에서 as 'at' (English analogy) — the split is destination vs action, not preposition translation
Forgetting that 에 also marks TIME of an event — 세 시에 만나요 (let's meet at 3) uses the same 에

drill.answer: 에서 (reading is an action at the library)

units.title: Other key particles — 도, 만, 의
units.goal: Add nuance (also / only / 's) using the most common non-case particles.
units.explanation: Beyond case-marking particles (은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서), three add semantic flavour: 도 ('also / too'), 만 ('only / just'), and 의 ('s / of'). 도 and 만 REPLACE 은/는 / 이/가 / 을/를 when attached — you don't stack them ('I too' = 저도, not 저는도). 도 and 만 attach with no allomorph (저도, 저만, 책도, 책만). 의 (possessive) attaches between two nouns: 친구의 책 (friend's book). In casual speech, 의 is usually dropped: 친구 책. 의 is pronounced 에 [e] when used as a possessive marker — a common surprise for learners.

endings.possessive: 친구 + 의 + 책 → 친구의 책 (friend's book)
endings.stacking rule: 도/만 REPLACE 은/는/이/가/을/를 — never stack as 저는도 or 저를만

common_errors: Stacking 도 on top of a case particle — 저는도 (wrong); use 저도
Stacking 만 on top of a case particle — 저를만 (wrong); use 저만 (and add a different particle later if the case is essential)
Pronouncing 의 as [의] when it's a possessive — natives pronounce it [에]: 친구의 = 'chin-gu-e', not 'chin-gu-eui'
Dropping 의 inappropriately — usually fine in casual speech (친구 책) but in headlines, signs, or formal writing 의 is expected

drill.prompt: Translate 'I am Korean too.' — 저___ 한국 사람이에요.
Translate 'Only my friend came.' — 친구___ 왔어요.
How is the possessive 의 pronounced in 친구의?

units.title: Verb conjugation — present tense (해요-form)
units.goal: Conjugate any verb or adjective into polite present (해요-form), including the main irregulars.
units.explanation: The polite present (해요체) is the everyday workhorse register. Algorithm: drop the dictionary -다 to get the stem, then add -아요 if the LAST vowel in the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ (yang/'bright' vowels), or -어요 otherwise. Stems ending in -하다 collapse to -해요. Vowel-end stems often contract: 가 + 아요 → 가요 (a+a fuses), 오 + 아요 → 와요, 마시 + 어요 → 마셔요, 배우 + 어요 → 배워요. The same form covers statement, question (rising intonation), suggestion ('let's'), and mild command — intonation and context disambiguate. Korean verbs do NOT change for subject person or number; the conjugated form 가요 means I/you/he/she/we/they go(es) depending on context.

endings.yang vowel stem (ㅏ/ㅗ): stem + 아요 → 가다 → 가요, 보다 → 봐요
endings.other stem: stem + 어요 → 먹다 → 먹어요, 마시다 → 마셔요
endings.vowel-fusion examples: 가 + 아요 → 가요, 오 + 아요 → 와요, 보 + 아요 → 봐요, 마시 + 어요 → 마셔요, 배우 + 어요 → 배워요

examples.target: 물을 마셔요. (마시다 + 어요 → 마셔요, vowel fusion)

common_errors: Picking the wrong vowel ending — 먹다 is consonant-end and the LAST vowel is ㅓ, so it's 먹어요, NOT 먹아요
Forgetting -하다 → -해요 — 공부하다 becomes 공부해요, not 공부하아요
Missing vowel fusion — 가다 + 아요 is 가요 (NOT 가아요); 보다 + 아요 is 봐요 (NOT 보아요)
Treating ㄷ-irregular verbs as regular — 듣다 (to listen) → 들어요, not 듣어요; 걷다 (to walk) → 걸어요. The ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending. Same trap with ㅂ-irregular (덥다 → 더워요) and ㅡ-deletion (예쁘다 → 예뻐요)

drill.prompt: Conjugate 예쁘다 (to be pretty) to polite present (ㅡ-deletion).
Conjugate 덥다 (to be hot) to polite present (ㅂ-irregular).

units.title: Past tense — 았/었어요 (vowel harmony)
units.goal: Form the polite past tense for any verb, with correct vowel-harmony allomorph and contractions.
units.explanation: The past-tense morpheme is -았- (after yang vowels ㅏ/ㅗ) or -었- (after all other vowels), inserted between the stem and the polite ending -어요. So the full pattern is: stem + 았어요 / 었어요. -하다 verbs collapse to -했어요. Vowel fusion in the past mirrors the present: 가다 → 가 + 았어요 → 갔어요, 오다 → 와 + ㅆ어요 → 왔어요, 마시다 → 마셔 + ㅆ어요 → 마셨어요. The double ㅆ (sang-shieut) at the start of 어요 is the diagnostic feature of past tense — if you see 았어 / 었어 / 했어 in a verb, it's past.

endings.yang vowel stem (ㅏ/ㅗ): stem + 았어요 → 가다 → 갔어요, 보다 → 봤어요
endings.other stem: stem + 었어요 → 먹다 → 먹었어요, 마시다 → 마셨어요
endings.contractions: 가 + 았어요 → 갔어요 (a+a fuses, ㅆ keeps past marker), 오 + 았어요 → 왔어요, 마시 + 었어요 → 마셨어요, 배우 + 었어요 → 배웠어요

examples.target: 음악을 들었어요. (듣다 → 들었어요, ㄷ-irregular keeps the ㄹ shift)

common_errors: Wrong vowel harmony — 먹다 → 먹았어요 (wrong); the last stem vowel is ㅓ so it's 먹었어요
Forgetting the contraction — 가다 + 았어요 fuses to 갔어요 (one block), NOT 가았어요 (two blocks)
Adding 았/었 to -하다 instead of swapping — 공부하았어요 (wrong); use 공부했어요
Confusing 았어요 (past) with 아요 (present) when listening — the doubled ㅆ is the audible cue: 'gat-sseo-yo' vs 'ga-yo'

drill.answer: 먹었어요 (먹- has ㅓ vowel → 었어요, not 았어요)

units.title: Future & probability — -겠어요 and -(으)ㄹ 거예요
units.goal: Express future intent, prediction, and probability using the two main future patterns.
units.explanation: Korean has two future-ish constructions used in different ways. -겠어요 attaches to ANY verb stem (가다 → 가겠어요, 먹다 → 먹겠어요) and conveys (a) speaker's immediate intent ('I shall'), (b) conjecture / 'must be' ('it must be cold'), or (c) polite hedging in service speech (잘 먹겠습니다 'I'll eat well' before a meal). -(으)ㄹ 거예요 attaches with the bridging vowel rule — vowel-end stems take -ㄹ 거예요 (가다 → 갈 거예요), consonant-end stems take -을 거예요 (먹다 → 먹을 거예요) — and conveys planned future or prediction ('I will / it will'). For first-person plans -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is more natural; -겠어요 is more 'I shall (right now)' or 'it must be'.

endings.-겠어요 (intent / conjecture / hedge): 가다 → 가겠어요, 먹다 → 먹겠어요, 덥다 → 덥겠어요 ('must be hot')
endings.-(으)ㄹ 거예요, vowel-end stem: 가다 → 갈 거예요, 마시다 → 마실 거예요
endings.-(으)ㄹ 거예요, consonant-end stem: 먹다 → 먹을 거예요, 읽다 → 읽을 거예요
endings.service-speech idioms: 잘 먹겠습니다 ('I'll eat well' before meal), 잘 가겠습니다, 알겠습니다 ('I understand')

examples.en: I will go to Korea tomorrow. (plan)
It looks like it'll rain today. (conjecture)
I'll eat well. (set phrase before meals)

common_errors: Using -겠어요 for ordinary planned future — 'I'll go tomorrow' is naturally 내일 갈 거예요, not 내일 가겠어요 (which sounds like 'I shall go right now')
Forgetting the bridge vowel for consonant-end stems — 먹다 → 먹ㄹ거예요 (wrong); correct is 먹을 거예요
Translating -겠어요 always as 'will' — it equally serves as 'must be' / 'looks like' for conjecture
Writing -ㄹ거예요 as one block — there's a space: 갈 거예요, 먹을 거예요

drill.prompt: Translate 'It must be cold today.' using 춥다 (to be cold).
Translate the set phrase 'I'll eat well.' before a meal.
Fix: 내일 학교에 가겠어요. (rendering as 'I plan to go tomorrow')

units.title: Negation — 안 / 못 / -지 않다
units.goal: Negate any verb three different ways and pick the right one for the meaning.
units.explanation: Korean has two short-form negators that sit BEFORE the verb — 안 (don't / not, choice) and 못 (can't, inability/external block) — and one long-form construction -지 않다 (the same as 안, attached to the stem). 안 negates by choice: 저는 안 가요 ('I'm not going / I don't go'). 못 negates by inability or external blocker: 저는 못 가요 ('I can't go — something stops me'). -하다 verbs split for 안: 공부 안 해요 (the 안 wedges between the noun and 하다), not 안 공부해요. The long form -지 않다 works on any verb identically to 안: 가지 않아요 = 안 가요. -지 못하다 is the long-form 못. Long forms feel slightly more formal/written.

endings.안 (choice negation): 안 + verb → 안 가요 (I don't go)
endings.못 (inability): 못 + verb → 못 가요 (I can't go)
endings.-하다 split with 안: 공부 안 해요 / 공부 못 해요 — 안/못 goes BEFORE 하다, NOT before the noun
endings.long form 안: stem + -지 않다 → 가지 않아요 / 먹지 않아요
endings.long form 못: stem + -지 못하다 → 가지 못해요 / 먹지 못해요

examples.en: I don't go / I'm not going.
I can't speak Korean. (-하다 split, fused word for skill-can't)
I don't watch that movie. (long form)

common_errors: Putting 안 in front of -하다 verbs as a unit — 안 공부해요 sounds awkward; native preference is 공부 안 해요 (also written 공부안해요)
Using 안 when you mean 'can't' — saying 안 가요 to your boss when you mean 'I'm unable to go' will sound like refusal; use 못 가요
Mixing forms — 안 가지 않아요 is doubly negated (rare and confusing); pick one form per verb
Treating 못 as rude — it's neutral and very common; 안 is sometimes more confrontational because it signals choice

drill.prompt: Translate 'I don't eat.' using short 안. (먹다)
Translate 'I can't eat.' using short 못. (먹다)
Convert 안 가요 to long form.
Convert 못 먹어요 to long form.
Pick the right negator: 'I'm too busy to come' — 못 와요 / 안 와요?
Pick the right negator: 'I just don't like it, so I won't' — 못 / 안?

units.title: Honorifics intro — -시- infix, 께서, 께
units.goal: Recognise and use the basic subject-honorific machinery for respected people.
units.explanation: Korean has TWO orthogonal politeness axes: speech LEVEL (해 / 해요 / 합니다 — about the LISTENER) and HONORIFICS (about the SUBJECT of the verb). When the subject of the sentence deserves respect (your boss, an elder, a customer's parent), insert -시- into the verb between the stem and the ending: 가다 → 가시다 → 가세요 / 가십니다. The subject particle 이/가 is replaced by the honorific 께서 (가다 → 어머니께서 가세요 — Mother goes). The indirect-object particle 에게 is replaced by 께. Some verbs have suppletive honorific forms: 먹다 → 드시다 (eat → dine), 자다 → 주무시다 (sleep → repose), 있다 → 계시다 (exist/stay → reside), 말하다 → 말씀하시다 (speak → discourse). Honorifics apply to the SUBJECT regardless of speech level — your boss can be subject-honorific while you're still in 해요 register: 사장님이 가세요.

examples.en: I give Mother a present. (께 + suppletive 드리다)

examples.target: 안녕히 가세요. (literally 'please go peacefully', built on this pattern)

common_errors: Confusing honorifics (about the subject) with speech level (about the listener) — your friend listening can be 해, but if you're talking ABOUT your boss to that friend, the boss still gets -시-
Honoring YOURSELF — 저는 가세요 is wrong (humble subject + honorific verb is contradictory); use 저는 가요
Using -시- with suppletive verbs — 먹다 has 드시다, NOT 먹으세요 for honored eaters (technically grammatical but suppletive is preferred)
Forgetting 께서 / 께 — using 이/가 / 에게 with an honored subject mixes registers oddly

drill.prompt: Honorific polite of 있다 (suppletive, 'to be at / reside').
Replace 이/가 with the honorific marker: 어머니___ 가세요.
Replace 에게 with the honorific indirect-object marker: 선생님___ 드려요.

units.title: Questions — endings -까? / -요? / intonation
units.goal: Form yes/no and wh-questions in each speech level.
units.explanation: Korean questions don't reorder words — there's no English-style subject-verb inversion. Instead, the verb's ENDING changes (formal level only) or intonation rises (polite and intimate). In formal 합쇼체, statements end -ㅂ니다 / -습니다 and questions end -ㅂ니까? / -습니까? (가다 → 갑니다 / 갑니까?). In polite 해요체, statements and questions look identical — only rising intonation distinguishes: 가요. vs 가요? Likewise for intimate 해체: 가. vs 가? Wh-words (뭐, 누가, 어디, 언제, 왜, 어떻게, 몇) stay IN PLACE — Korean doesn't front them like English does: '어디 가요?' is literally 'where go?', not 'where do you go?'. The interrogative particle 까 only attaches in formal speech.

endings.wh-word placement: 어디 가요? (where go?) — wh-word stays in its natural position

examples.en: Where are you going? — I'm going to school. (formal)
Where are you going? — I'm going to school. (polite)
When did you come to Korea?

common_errors: Adding -까 to polite/intimate questions — 가요까? is wrong; -까 only attaches in formal -ㅂ니까/-습니까
Fronting the wh-word like English — '어디 너는 가요?' sounds translated; natives say '너는 어디 가요?' or '어디 가요?'
Using -요 in formal questions — 갑니다요? is wrong; formal-question uses 갑니까?
Forgetting that 무엇 + 이에요 contracts to 뭐예요 in everyday speech (이름이 뭐예요?, not 이름이 무엇이에요?)

drill.prompt: Convert 가요. to a polite question.
Convert 갑니다. to a formal question.
Convert 먹어. to an intimate question.
Translate 'What do you eat?' (polite, use 뭐)

drill.answer: 친구가 어디에 있어요? (or 친구 어디 있어요?)
가요? (drop the 까 — 까 only in formal)
너는 어디 가요? (don't front the wh-word past the subject)

drill.prompt: Translate 'When did you come?' using 언제 + 오다 polite past question.
